> 大壯。利貞。

Hexagram 34 is about great strength, and it spends four of its six lines describing a ram stuck in a fence.

## 壯, and what 大 points to

壯: strong, powerful.

And 大 here is not size. 大者，陽也 — the "great" in the name is yang.

So 大壯 is not "a large force." It is a great quantity of the firm, active line — four solid lines rising from the bottom, pushing up against two yielding ones.

Which is the whole problem of the hexagram: strength in quantity, with nowhere legitimate to go.

## 趾 and 輹

初九 壯于趾，征凶，有孚.

趾: the toe. Strength at the very bottom, in the feet, with a shallow base.

征凶 — advancing is bad — 有孚, and it is certain.

九四 貞吉，悔亡；藩決不羸，壯于大輿之輹 — the fence breaks, the horns come free, and the strength is in the binding of the great carriage.

And here the book has to make a distinction it has been building for several chapters:

| character | where | what it is | if it fails |
|---|---|---|---|
| 輻 | 小畜九三 | the spokes, rim to hub | the wheel comes apart; the cart cannot move |
| 輹 | 大畜九二 | the binding between box and axle | box and axle separate; nothing can be carried |
| 輹 | 大壯九四 | the same binding | bound firmly, so it can carry far |

The first two are 說 — removed. This one is 壯 — strong.

Same part: take it out and the cart is useless; make it strong and the cart carries.

Which is the only positive use of 輹 in the whole book, and it is placed precisely where the hexagram's strength finally becomes useful.

## 羝羊觸藩，羸其角

A ram is an animal that pushes; 藩 is a fence — a boundary, a limit, a rule.

And the ram pushes into the fence and gets its horns caught: 羸, bound up, entangled.

The image appears twice — 九三 and 上六 — and the second one states the outcome plainly: 不能退，不能遂，無攸利.

Cannot retreat, cannot advance, and nothing is gained.

So the two ends of the hexagram both show the same failure: force applied to a boundary. The difference is that at line 3 the ram still believes it will get through, and at line 6 it knows it will not.

## 小人用壯，君子用罔

九三: the small man uses his strength; the noble uses 罔.

罔 is 無 — nothing. (Another reading takes it as 網, a net; this book takes "nothing.")

So the noble has the strength and behaves as if he did not.

Which is the only line in the hexagram that offers a way out of the ram's position, and it is available at the exact point of maximum pressure.

## 喪羊于易，無悔

六五: losing the ram at 易 — the level open ground, the plain. (Another reading: 疆埸, the border.)

Losing the sheep in the open, and no regret.

At the ruler's place, the yielding line gives up the animal altogether. Which the text does not mourn: the ram was the problem.

## 非禮弗履

The 象: 君子以非禮弗履.

履 is not "walk" — it is to tread, to step onto.

So: what does not belong to one's measure is not stepped on. The boundary in the hexagram is not a wall built to stop the ram; it is a place one declines to put one's foot.

## The test

Take a strength you have — a budget, a mandate, a majority. Ask whether it is 壯于趾 (all in the feet) or 壯于輹 (bound where the load is carried). The difference is not the amount. It is whether the force is attached to the thing that carries weight, or only to the part that pushes.
